patient.chief_complaint: Progressive ascending weakness with areflexia in an HIV-positive woman with CD4 380 and undetectable viral load.
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. L. is a 35-year-old HIV-positive woman on antiretroviral therapy presenting with a 9-day history of ascending weakness. Her HIV is well-controlled (CD4 380, VL undetectable) on Biktarvy. She had a gastrointestinal illness 3 weeks ago lasting 4 days. Nine days ago, she developed bilateral foot paresthesias that rapidly ascended. She has progressive bilateral leg weakness and cannot walk without support. She notes left facial weakness and mild left ptosis. She has mild dysphagia for thin liquids. She has been adherent to her antiretrovirals. She denies any opportunistic infections, night sweats, weight loss, or rashes. Emergency providers raised concern about HIV-associated neuromuscular disease, but the acute tempo, antecedent infection, and areflexia strongly suggest GBS. The diagnostic challenge: her HIV status and the mild CSF pleocytosis may suggest HIV-associated GBS (which can present with CSF pleocytosis unlike typical GBS).

results.title: GBS in HIV-infected patients: clinical characteristics
results.finding: GBS has been reported in HIV-infected individuals across a range of CD4 counts. CSF pleocytosis (up to 50 mononuclear cells) has been documented in this population and may differ from the typical albuminocytologic dissociation pattern seen in HIV-negative patients.

results.title: Treatment of GBS in HIV-infected patients
results.finding: Published case series and guidelines indicate IVIG and plasmapheresis are used for GBS treatment in HIV-infected patients; dosing is generally consistent with standard regimens. Concurrent antiretroviral therapy is typically continued.

output.summary: GBS in HIV-infected patients is a recognized clinical entity. The CSF profile may differ from classic GBS, with mononuclear pleocytosis reported in this population. Published evidence supports use of IVIG or plasmapheresis. Clinical correlation with individual patient findings is required.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Guillain-Barré syndrome, AIDP — HIV-associated (with CSF pleocytosis)

differential.key_features: HIV is associated with both acute (GBS-like) and chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathies; differentiation depends on course (<4 weeks vs >8 weeks).

CD4 380 makes severe opportunistic disease less likely, but CMV testing and CSF PCR are warranted given pleocytosis; CMV polyradiculitis typically shows marked CSF neutrophilic pleocytosis and lower CD4.
Possible HIV coinfection; RPR / FTA-ABS and CSF VDRL warranted but not the primary picture without other features.
Biktarvy regimen has low neuropathy risk; areflexia and acute progression do not fit a chronic toxic axonal pattern.
No endemic exposure or erythema migrans; serology unsupported.

optimal_actions.action: Obtain CBC, CMP, HIV, anti-GM1/anti-GQ1b ganglioside antibodies, and stool culture / Campylobacter serology if recent diarrhea
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Mild leukocytosis / elevated inflammatory markers reflecting antecedent infection; ganglioside antibodies for variant typing; trigger identification (Campylobacter, CMV, EBV, Mycoplasma, HIV)

optimal_actions.action: Order nerve conduction studies and needle EMG (EMG/NCS)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Demyelinating pattern (prolonged DML, conduction block, reduced CV, absent F-waves) consistent with AIDP, or reduced CMAP amplitudes in axonal variants (AMAN/AMSAN)

optimal_actions.action: Perform lumbar puncture for CSF analysis
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Albuminocytologic dissociation — elevated protein with cell count <10/μL; may be normal in the first week of illness

optimal_actions.action: Order bedside respiratory function testing (FVC, MIP/MEP, NIF) and repeat every 4–6 hours
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Baseline and serial FVC, MIP/MEP, NIF; deterioration to FVC <20 mL/kg, MIP worse than -30 cmH2O, or VC <40% predicted triggers ICU transfer / intubation

optimal_actions.action: Search the medical literature for IVIG vs plasma exchange evidence to guide disease-modifying therapy
optimal_actions.expected_finding: IVIG (0.4 g/kg/day x 5 days) and plasma exchange are equivalently effective first-line therapies; combination not superior

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions / contraindications for IVIG (renal function, IgA deficiency screen) and/or plasma exchange (coagulation, calcium, hemodynamics)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Confirmation that IVIG can be given safely (no severe renal impairment, no IgA deficiency) or that plasma exchange is appropriate (adequate vascular access, stable coagulation)

optimal_actions.action: Obtain a 12-lead ECG to screen for autonomic dysrhythmias and baseline QTc
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Sinus tachycardia or bradycardia; conduction or repolarisation abnormalities reflecting autonomic involvement

optimal_actions.action: Initiate continuous cardiac telemetry for the first 1–2 weeks for moderate/severe disease — autonomic instability (bradyarrhythmias, BP lability) is common
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Documentation of sinus pauses, bradyarrhythmias, BP lability, or non-sustained tachyarrhythmias

useless_tools.rationale: GBS is a peripheral nerve / nerve-root disorder; EEG has no role in diagnosis unless atypical CNS features (encephalopathy, seizures) are present.
Echocardiography is not indicated in typical GBS; reserve for pre-existing cardiac disease or unexplained hemodynamic instability after autonomic causes are excluded.
Head CT contributes no diagnostic information in GBS; the disease is peripheral and CT does not visualise nerve roots reliably.
Functional / metabolic brain imaging adds no value in a peripheral demyelinating syndrome.
Cerebrovascular imaging is not indicated in a peripheral neuropathy without focal cerebral signs.
Brain MRI is reserved for atypical features (encephalopathy, CNS signs, transverse myelitis on differential). In classic GBS it does not aid diagnosis.

sequence_constraints.reason: Document respiratory status (FVC/NIF) before committing to IVIG vs plasma exchange — severe respiratory compromise mandates ICU triage and may influence treatment choice and timing.
Renal function, IgA screen, and CBC must be reviewed before IVIG to mitigate renal failure, anaphylaxis (IgA-deficient patients), and aseptic meningitis risk.

critical_actions: Continue antiretroviral therapy; consult ID for HIV comanagement.
Initiate IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days (preferred over PLEX in HIV given immune considerations).
Monitor respiratory function and autonomic status closely.
CSF CMV PCR, VDRL, and cytology to rule out opportunistic / coinfection polyradiculitis given pleocytosis.
contraindicated_actions: Do not stop antiretrovirals during the acute phase.
Do not give corticosteroids as monotherapy.
Do not assume pleocytosis excludes GBS — HIV-associated GBS classically shows CSF pleocytosis.
key_reasoning_points: HIV-associated GBS is a well-described entity; CSF pleocytosis (10–50 WBC/μL) is expected and does NOT rule out GBS.
Distinguishing HIV-related acute polyneuropathy from opportunistic CMV polyradiculitis is critical — CMV typically has lower CD4 and marked neutrophilic pleocytosis.
Ganglioside antibody panel and antecedent infection workup remain important even in HIV-positive patients.
Treatment with IVIG is preferred over PLEX in HIV to avoid removing circulating antiretroviral medication.

red_herrings.data_point: CSF pleocytosis above the classic GBS expectation
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggest opportunistic / infectious polyradiculitis rather than HIV-associated GBS.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Mild-moderate CSF pleocytosis is well-recognised in HIV-associated GBS at preserved CD4 counts; in the absence of CMV PCR positivity it does not redirect the diagnosis.
